issues.legal_issue: A civil suit cannot be used to set aside or modify a tax assessment made under the governing tax legislation.
material_facts: The plaintiffs sued to have tax assessments against their family declared unenforceable against property and to restrain the revenue authorities from selling or confirming sales of that property.
The tax assessments had been made under the tax legislation, and the plaintiffs alleged that the tax officer had failed to inquire into a claimed partition.
issues.conclusion: The suit was barred insofar as it sought to set aside or modify the assessments; any error in assessment had to be addressed through the remedies provided by the tax legislation.
issues.legal_principle: Section 67 of the Indian Income-Tax Act, 1922 bars a civil suit to set aside or modify an assessment made under that Act. The assessment procedure and remedies are prescribed by the Act, including an appeal under section 30. Relying on Commissioner of Income-tax v. Tribune Trust, Lahore, the Court held that the taxpayer’s remedies must be found within the Act.

predicates.tax_assessment_challenge_suit: A claimant brings a civil suit seeking to invalidate or alter a tax assessment.
predicates.assessment_made_under_tax_law: The challenged assessment was made by a tax authority under the governing tax legislation.
predicates.civil_suit_barred: The civil suit cannot be used to set aside or modify the assessment.

issues.definition: When a civil suit seeks to invalidate or alter an assessment made under tax legislation, the suit is barred from providing that relief.

issues.legal_issue: A family’s tax liability that accrued while it was joint remains enforceable against its members after a later partition.
material_facts: The family business and its income belonged to the joint family during the relevant accounting years.
The tax liability arose no later than the close of those accounting years, before the claimed partition.
No order recording partition was made under section 25A(1), although a claim of partition had been brought to the tax officer’s attention.
The assessments were made on the family as an undivided family.
issues.conclusion: The family was properly assessed as undivided in the absence of an order recording partition; even if such an order had been made, the members would remain jointly and severally liable for the tax assessed on the family income.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 25A of the Indian Income-Tax Act, 1922, tax liability arises from the income and accrues no later than the close of the accounting year; later quantification does not postpone that liability, as explained in Wallace Brothers & Co. Ltd. v. Commissioner of Income-tax. Where liability arose while the family was joint, a later partition does not displace the family tax liability. Under section 25A(3), without an order recording partition the family is deemed to continue as undivided for the Act. If partition is recorded under section 25A(1), section 25A(2) apportions liability but its proviso preserves the members’ joint and several liability for tax assessed on the family income. The Court also relied on Sardar Bahadur Sir Sunder Singh Majithia v. Commissioner of Income-tax in describing the section’s operation.

predicates.family_tax_liability: A tax liability is assessed on income received by a family as a family.
predicates.liability_accrued_during_joint_status: The tax liability arose while the family still existed as a joint family.
predicates.family_tax_debt_remains_enforceable_agai: The family tax debt remains enforceable against family members despite a later partition.

issues.definition: If a family tax liability accrued while the family was joint, the debt remains enforceable against its members after a later partition.

issues.legal_issue: Property purchased in the names of family members may be treated as joint-family property when the evidence supports an inference that joint-family funds paid for it.
material_facts: The properties were conveyed in the names of two sons, so the taxing authorities initially bore the burden of showing that they were purchased for the joint family or with joint-family funds.
The sons’ claim that their grandmother provided the purchase money was unsupported by documents and rested on testimony found unreliable and improbable.
The sons had no other source of income, the father had made substantial profits in the family business, and he paid a substantial part of the purchase price to the vendors.

There was evidence of an outstanding attachment against family property at the time of purchase, supporting the inference that the father used the sons’ names to protect the properties from creditors.
issues.conclusion: The evidence supported the finding that the properties were purchased with joint-family funds and belonged to the joint family, making them liable to attachment and sale for the family’s tax liability.
issues.legal_principle: The taxing authorities initially bore the burden of establishing that property conveyed in the sons’ names was acquired for the family or with family funds. The Court held that where both sides have led evidence, abstract considerations of onus give way to deciding the truth from the evidence as a whole. It was a legitimate inference that the father paid for the properties from joint-family earnings when the alleged alternative source of funds was disbelieved and the other circumstances supported that inference.

rule.if: tax_property_recovery_dispute and property_purchased_in_family_members_names and alleged_independent_funding_discredited and family_manager_paid_purchase_money and purchasers_lacked_other_income

predicates.tax_property_recovery_dispute: A dispute concerns whether property may be reached to recover tax assessed on a family.
predicates.property_purchased_in_family_members_nam: Property was conveyed in the names of members of the family rather than in the family’s name.
predicates.alleged_independent_funding_discredited: The evidence offered to show that an independent source supplied the purchase money was found unreliable.
predicates.family_manager_paid_purchase_money: The family manager paid a substantial part of the purchase price.
predicates.purchasers_lacked_other_income: The named purchasers had no other source of income capable of explaining the purchase.
predicates.property_treated_as_joint_family_propert: The property is treated as belonging to the joint family.

issues.definition: In a tax-property recovery dispute, property in family members’ names is treated as joint-family property when the asserted independent funding is discredited, the family manager paid for it, and the purchasers lacked other income.

issues.legal_issue: Execution and registration of a partition deed do not establish that the partition was intended to operate when the surrounding evidence shows that it was merely nominal.
material_facts: The partition deed was executed shortly after a creditor obtained a decree against the father.
The evidence showed that the father continued to manage the property and collect rents after the deed, while the family continued living together.
The mother, who was named as guardian in the deed, did not manage the property and did not know which properties had been allotted to the sons.

The father instigated and prosecuted the suits concerning the property, and the circumstances supported the conclusion that the deed was intended to protect property from creditors and tax authorities rather than to effect a real division.
issues.conclusion: The deed was a sham transaction that was never intended to be acted upon; the sons could not rely on it to set aside the execution-related order, and both appeals were dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: Whether a partition deed was intended to be effective is determined from the evidence and surrounding circumstances; execution or registration alone is not decisive. Continued management by the father, continued family life, the absence of actual management by the purported guardian, the timing and purpose of the deed, and the parties’ conduct supported the finding that the deed was nominal. The Court did not decide the disputed procedural question whether, after a genuine partition, a creditor must bring a separate suit or may proceed in execution against a son’s interest. It referred to the differing approaches in Schwebo K.S.R.M. Firm v. Subbiah, Katragadda China Ramayya v. Chiruvella Venkataraju, and Ganpatrao Vishwanathappa v. Bhimrao Sahibrao, and to S.M. Jakati v. S.M. Borkar on the continuing pious obligation, but found it unnecessary to resolve that question because the partition was sham.

rule.if: execution_proceeding_challenge and partition_deed_executed_or_registered and father_continued_managing_property and family_continued_living_together and deed_contrived_to_protect_property_from_creditors

predicates.execution_proceeding_challenge: A claimant challenges an order made in proceedings to execute a creditor’s decree against family property.
predicates.partition_deed_executed_or_registered: The family members executed or registered a deed purporting to partition their property.
predicates.father_continued_managing_property: The father continued to manage the property after the purported partition.
predicates.family_continued_living_together: The family continued living together after the purported partition.
predicates.deed_contrived_to_protect_property_from_: The circumstances show that the deed was made to keep property beyond creditors’ reach rather than to effect a real division.
predicates.partition_deed_is_nominal_and_unoperativ: The deed is treated as nominal and not as an operative partition.

issues.definition: In a challenge arising from execution proceedings, a purported partition is treated as nominal when the deed was made to shield property from creditors and the family’s conduct shows no actual division.
